Group of mainly aquatic [[Arthropod|arthropods]], traditionally ranked as the subphylum Crustacea. The name derives from the Latin *crustacea*, "those with shells." Crustaceans include decapods (shrimps, prawns, [[Crab|crabs]], [[Lobster|lobsters]], and crayfish), [[Krill|krill]], isopods, [[Barnacle|barnacles]], copepods, amphipods, and mantis shrimp.

The 67,000 described species range from *Stygotantulus stocki* at 0.1 mm (0.004 in) to the [[Japanese spider crab]], with a leg span of up to 3.8 m (12.5 ft) and a mass of 20 kg (44 lb). Crustaceans have an exoskeleton, which they molt to grow. They are distinguished from insects, myriapods, and chelicerates by biramous (two-parted) limbs and by larval forms such as the nauplius stage. The body has a head, thorax, and abdomen, and head and thorax may fuse into a cephalothorax under a carapace. Because hexapods (insects and entognathans) are now accepted as cladistically crustaceans, the two groups are combined in the clade Pancrustacea, which makes the traditional Crustacea paraphyletic.

Most crustaceans are free-living aquatic animals, but some are terrestrial (woodlice), some parasitic (fish lice), and some sessile (adult barnacles). The fossil record reaches back to the [[Cambrian]]. Krill and copepods may be the animals with the greatest biomass on the planet, and krill form the bottom layer of the Antarctic food chain. More than 7.9 million tons of crustaceans per year are harvested or farmed for human consumption, mostly shrimp and prawns. Some, such as the Chinese mitten crab, are significant invasive species. Their study is carcinology.

Practice and study of techniques for secure communication in the presence of adversaries; also called cryptology. Modern cryptography lies at the intersection of [[Mathematics|mathematics]], [[Computer science|computer science]], information security, electrical engineering, and physics. Its core concepts are data confidentiality, data integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation. Applications include electronic commerce, chip-based payment cards, digital currencies, passwords, secure messaging, and military communications.

Before the modern age, cryptography was effectively synonymous with [[Encryption|encryption]]: converting readable plaintext into unintelligible ciphertext that can be read only by reversing the process. A cipher is a pair of algorithms for encryption and decryption, controlled by a secret key. Early techniques included substitution ciphers such as the shift cipher attributed to [[Julius Caesar]]. Rotor cipher machines were developed in World War I, and computers in World War II made methods increasingly complex.

Symmetric systems, the only kind known until the 1970s, use one secret key to encrypt and decrypt. Asymmetric systems use a public key to encrypt and a related private key to decrypt, so parties can communicate without a shared secret. [[Public-key cryptography|Public-key cryptography]] is credited to Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman. In practice, asymmetric systems exchange a key, and a faster symmetric system such as AES then carries the communication. Modern algorithms rest on computational hardness assumptions.

Many governments classify cryptography as a weapon and limit its use or export. Critics have accused agencies such as the [[National Security Agency]] of pressing for deliberate weaknesses in standards, as in the unsuccessful Clipper chip initiative of the 1990s; the debate weighs privacy against national security.

Social behavior, institutions, and norms found in human societies, together with the knowledge, beliefs, arts, laws, customs, capabilities, attitudes, and habits of their members. Culture often originates from or is attributed to a specific region or location, and it is a central concept in [[Anthropology|anthropology]], which treats it as the range of phenomena transmitted through social learning.

Humans acquire culture through enculturation and [[Socialization|socialization]], and the diversity of cultures across societies reflects this. In 1871 the anthropologist E. B. Tylor defined it as "that complex whole which includes knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and any other capabilities and habits acquired by man as a member of society." The modern English word rests on a metaphor of the Roman orator [[Cicero]], who wrote of a cultivation of the soul (*cultura animi*); 18th-century German thinkers gave it most of its later meaning and often contrasted culture with civilization. Cultural norms codify acceptable conduct and serve as templates for expectations within a group. Sociological frameworks often divide culture into cognitive (ideas, beliefs, values), normative (rules and expectations), and material (artifacts and technology) components. Cultural universals found in all societies include art, music, dance, ritual, religion, tool use, cooking, shelter, and clothing. The capacity for symbolic culture is often linked to the evolution of behavioral modernity around 50,000 years ago and is often thought to be unique to humans, though some other species show simpler forms of social learning.

The word has several senses. In the humanities it has meant an individual's degree of cultivation in the arts, sciences, education, or manners, and it has been used to distinguish a high culture of social elites from the [[Popular culture|popular]], folk, or low culture of other classes. Mass culture refers to the mass-produced forms of consumer culture that emerged in the 20th century. As a count noun, a culture is the set of customs, traditions, and values of a community such as an ethnic group or nation; the term also describes a [[Subculture|subculture]] or counterculture within a society. [[Multiculturalism]] values peaceful coexistence and mutual respect among cultures.

Cultures change through internal forces both encouraging and resisting change, and through contact between societies. Raimon Panikkar identified 29 ways in which cultural change can occur, including evolution, reform, innovation, revolution, diffusion, borrowing, and syncretism.

Interpretations differ. Cultural relativism holds that cultures cannot easily be objectively ranked, since any evaluation is situated within a given value system. Other researchers argue that cultural practices causally influence economic prosperity, social stability, and individual behavior. Some schools of thought, such as [[Marxism]] and critical theory, argue that culture is used politically by elites to manipulate the proletariat. Organizations such as [[UNESCO]] work to preserve culture and cultural heritage.

Persian king, founder of the [[Achaemenid Empire]] (r. 559–530 BC). Also known as Cyrus II of Persia, he came from Anshan, in Persis. Around 550 BC he revolted against the Median king Astyages. He defeated [[Lydia]] in 546 BC and captured [[Babylon]] in 539 BC with minimal resistance, gaining control of Anatolia and the Fertile Crescent. His conquests created what became the largest empire in history up to that time. It reached its greatest extent later, under Darius the Great.

Cyrus allegedly died in battle against the Massagetae along the Syr Darya, according to Herodotus; Xenophon says he instead returned to the capital, Pasargadae. His son Cambyses II succeeded him and conquered Egypt, Nubia, and Cyrenaica.

Greek writers praised his tolerance toward the customs and religions of conquered peoples. The Cyrus Cylinder records his restoration of local cults and the repatriation of exiles, including the Jews. Some modern assessments hold that this was pragmatic toleration for administrative efficiency rather than ideological benevolence. In Judaism he is exalted for ending the [[Babylonian captivity]]; the Hebrew Bible describes the return to Judah and the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem. According to the Book of [[Isaiah]], he was anointed by Yahweh and designated "messiah," the only non-Jewish figure so revered.

Cyrus is credited with developing a central administration to govern the empire's satraps, a model said to have influenced later states. Later Persian empires viewed the Achaemenid era as an ideal to emulate, and his tomb at Pasargadae remains a site of reverence for many Iranians.

Deoxyribonucleic acid, a [[Polymer|polymer]] of two polynucleotide chains coiled in a double helix, which carries the genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth, and reproduction of all known organisms and many viruses. DNA and [[RNA|ribonucleic acid]] (RNA) are the two nucleic acids found in all life.

Each strand is a series of nucleotides, each made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), or thymine (T). The strands are antiparallel and held together by hydrogen bonds, which pair A with T and C with G. The double helix has a pitch of 34 ångströms (3.4 nm). The sequence of bases encodes genetic information; because both strands carry it, it can be replicated when they separate. Under the genetic code, RNA copies of DNA (transcription) specify the sequence of amino acids in [[Protein|proteins]] (translation).

In eukaryotes, DNA is organized into [[Chromosome|chromosomes]], stored mostly in the nucleus, with some in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Prokaryotes store DNA in the cytoplasm in circular chromosomes. The human genome comprises about 3 billion base pairs on 23 pairs of chromosomes; only about 1–2% consists of protein-coding genes, approximately 20,000 in total.

Friedrich Miescher first isolated DNA in 1869. In 1944 Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, and Maclyn McCarty showed that it is responsible for heredity in bacteria. In 1953 [[James Watson]] and [[Francis Crick]] proposed the double-helix model, building on X-ray data from [[Rosalind Franklin]] and Maurice Wilkins; it was published in *Nature*.

Structure built across a watercourse to impound water or restrict its flow, usually creating a [[Reservoir|reservoir]]. Dams are classified into four basic types: gravity dams, of concrete or masonry, which resist the water by their weight; embankment dams, large earthworks of rock, clay, sand, soil, or gravel; buttress dams, with a sloped concrete face supported by triangular buttresses; and arch dams, whose curved concrete wall transfers the water's weight to the valley walls. Natural dams include rockslide, volcanic, and beaver dams.

Dams serve [[Irrigation|irrigation]], [[Hydropower|hydropower]], water supply, flood management, recreation, inland navigation, and fish farming. About 20% of the world's arable land is irrigated with water from reservoirs behind dams. Many include locks, fish ladders, spillways, and outlets. The embankment dam is the most common type; it is cheaper than concrete and can sit on softer soils, but it is inherently permeable, and seepage can cause failure by "piping."

An early dam was Jawa Dam in modern Jordan, built around 3000 BC. The Hittite Empire built several dams in modern Turkey between the 17th and 13th centuries BC, and in the 1st century AD the [[Roman Empire]] began building masonry gravity dams. From the late 18th century, dam design became an engineering discipline rooted in science, and in the 20th century concrete and heavy machinery enabled many large projects. Over 58,000 large dams now operate worldwide.

Failures cause flooding and loss of life, as in the 1975 collapse of the Banqiao Dam in China. Dams can also disrupt ecosystems, trap sediment, and alter aquatic habitats. A dam may be removed if it is unsafe, no longer serves its purpose, or blocks fish migration or sediment flow.

Art form consisting of sequences of body movements with aesthetic and often symbolic value, either improvised or purposefully selected. Dance can be described by its [[Choreography|choreography]], its repertoire of movements, its historical period, or its place of origin. It is typically performed with [[Music|musical]] accompaniment.

Two common types of group dance are theatrical and participatory. Theatrical dance is intended primarily as a spectacle, usually performed on a stage by virtuoso dancers. It often tells a story, using mime, costume, and scenery. Examples include Western [[Ballet|ballet]] and [[Modern dance|modern dance]], classical Indian dance such as [[Bharatanatyam]], and Chinese and Japanese song and dance dramas such as the dragon dance. Either type may serve a social, ceremonial, competitive, erotic, martial, sacred, or liturgical function. Dance is also used as [[Exercise|exercise]] and as training for other sports, and it may be done alone for self-expression.

Archaeological evidence, including rock art at Bhimbetka in India, indicates that dance-like activities date back at least 10,000 years. Researchers have proposed that dance developed into a mechanism for social signaling, group coordination, and mate attraction. It was long presumed universal across human cultures, though some ethnographic studies have identified isolated groups with minimal formalized dance. Studies associate dancing with improved cardiovascular fitness, motor coordination, memory, and spatial awareness.

Italian poet, writer, and philosopher, author of the *Divine Comedy*. Born in [[Florence]] into a Guelph family, he fought with the Guelph cavalry at Campaldino on June 11, 1289, and joined the Physicians' and Apothecaries' Guild to take part in public life. In 1300 he served as a prior, amid conflicts between [[Guelphs and Ghibellines]]. In 1302 the victorious Black Guelphs condemned him on charges of barratry, corruption, and opposition to the pope. He was permanently exiled and faced a death sentence if he returned without paying a fine he refused. He wandered through Verona, Padua, and other courts, and died in [[Ravenna]] without reconciling with Florence.

At a time when [[Latin]] dominated scholarly writing, Dante wrote in his native Tuscan dialect. His *De vulgari eloquentia* was one of the first scholarly defenses of the vernacular. His use of Florentine in *The New Life* (1295) and the *Divine Comedy* helped establish the standardized [[Italian language]]; he is often called its "father," and in Italy *il Sommo Poeta* ("the Supreme Poet"). [[Petrarch]] and [[Giovanni Boccaccio|Boccaccio]] followed his precedent, and the three are called the *tre corone* ("three crowns") of Italian literature.

The *Divine Comedy*, begun around 1308, was originally titled *Comedìa*; Boccaccio later called it *Divina*. An allegorical journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, it synthesizes medieval theology, classical philosophy, and the poet's experience of exile. It is widely considered one of the most important poems of the Middle Ages. Dante is credited with the first use of *terza rima*, and influenced Geoffrey Chaucer, John Milton, and Alfred Tennyson.

Unit of time equal to one full rotation of the [[Earth]] with respect to the Sun, averaging 24 hours (86,400 seconds). The daily cycle drives [[Circadian rhythm|circadian rhythms]] in many organisms.

Days are organized into [[Calendar|calendars]], grouped into weeks, months, and years. In common usage a day starts at midnight. Because the time of midnight varies between locations, [[Time zone|time zones]] provide a uniform standard time; they began to be adopted in the middle of the 19th century with railroads, and as of 2015, 40 were in use, all defined as offsets from [[Coordinated Universal Time]]. The Jewish religious calendar counts days from sunset, and in astronomy a day begins at noon.

Several definitions serve specific purposes. The SI day is exactly 86,400 seconds. A fictitious mean Sun moving at constant speed defines the mean solar day, removing the yearly variation caused by Earth's orbit and axial tilt. A sidereal day, measured against the celestial background, lasts 23 hours, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds. Tidal interactions with the Moon are lengthening Earth's day by about 2.3 milliseconds per century.

On other bodies a day is a full rotation with respect to the star. The solar day on [[Mercury (planet)|Mercury]] is 176 Earth days, longer than its year of 88 days; on [[Venus]] it is 117 Earth days, shorter than its year of 225 days. [[Jupiter]] has a day of approximately 10 hours, and a solar day on Mars is about 24 hours and 37 minutes.

Irreversible cessation of the biological functions that sustain a living organism. After death, organisms stop exhibiting behavior and generally begin to decompose. Death can occur at any stage of development, and entropy, the tendency toward disorder, can contribute to the breakdown of living systems. Clinical death, the stopping of breathing and heartbeat, may in some cases be reversed, sometimes producing a near-death experience.

Defining death is difficult, partly because there is little consensus on how to define life and because life functions do not cease simultaneously across organ systems. Death was originally defined as the end of breathing and heartbeat, but cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) meant that this state was no longer strictly irreversible. For organisms with a brain, death can instead be focused on that organ. Some hold that all brain functions must cease; others hold that a person whose personality and identity are irretrievably lost should be considered dead even if the brainstem is alive. [[Brain death]] is sometimes used as a legal definition. It is diagnosed through clinical examination, apnea testing, and exclusion of confounding factors such as hypothermia or drug effects. Controversies include the rare reports of recovery and the ethics of withdrawing life support.

In the natural world, organisms die through predation, parasitism, competition, starvation, dehydration, natural disasters, disease, or old age. Some organisms, such as the immortal jellyfish, are biologically immortal yet can still die from other causes. Selective pressures cause organisms with unfavorable traits to die off, and [[Natural selection]] drives living things to avoid death. When all members of a clade have died, it is extinct; extinction events are periods of mass death in many species worldwide that cause a global loss of biodiversity.

As of the early 21st century, 56 million people die per year. As of 2022, an estimated almost 110 billion humans had died, roughly 94% of all humans to have ever lived. The most common reason is aging, and the most common cause is [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]]. An autopsy can be done to determine cause of death. Biogerontology seeks ways to eliminate death by natural aging, and humans attempt to reach their maximum lifespan through lifestyle changes such as calorie reduction, diet, and exercise. Humans also die through [[Suicide|suicide]], homicide, punishment for crimes, and war.

Because humans are aware of death, it is a central part of the human condition and universal to human culture. It has motivated religious, spiritual, ethical, and legal responses. Many cultures hold that individuals survive death in an [[Afterlife|afterlife]], as spirits, or through reincarnation, while monist forms of thought such as materialism and physicalism take other views. Customs for honoring the body include the [[Funeral|funeral]], cremation, and sky burial, and family and friends usually go through a process of grieving. The study of death is known as thanatology.
